{{Short description|Mathematical concept}}
{{About|the mathematical concept|the accent|ring (diacritic)}}

{{Ring theory sidebar}}

In mathematics, an '''overring''' of an [[integral domain]] contains the integral domain, and the integral domain's [[field of fractions]] contains the overring.  Overrings provide an improved understanding of different types of rings and [[Domain (ring theory)|domains]].

==Definition==
<em>In this article, all [[Ring (mathematics)|rings]] are [[commutative ring]]s, and ring and overring share the same [[identity element]].</em>

Let <math display="inline">Q(A)</math> represent the field of fractions of an integral domain <math display="inline">A</math>.   Ring <math display="inline">B</math> is an overring of integral domain <math display="inline">A</math> if <math display="inline">A</math> is a [[subring]] of <math display="inline">B</math> and <math display="inline">B</math> is a subring of the field of fractions <math display="inline">Q(A)</math>;{{sfn|Fontana|Papick|2002}}{{rp|167}} the relationship is <math display="inline">A \subseteq B \subseteq Q(A) </math>.{{sfn|Papick|1978}}{{rp|373}}

==Properties==
===Ring of fractions===
The rings <math display="inline">R_{A},S_{A},T_{A}</math> are the <em>[[Total ring of fractions|rings of fractions]]</em> of rings <math display="inline">R,S,T</math> by <em>[[Localization (commutative algebra)|multiplicative set]]</em> <math display="inline">A</math>.{{sfn|Zariski|Samuel|1965}}{{rp|46}}  Assume <math display="inline">T</math> is an overring of <math display="inline">R</math> and <math display="inline">A</math> is a multiplicative set in <math display="inline">R</math>.  The ring <math display="inline">T_{A}</math> is an overring of <math display="inline">R_{A}</math>.  The ring <math display="inline">T_{A}</math> is the [[total ring of fractions]] of <math display="inline">R_{A}</math> if every  [[Unit (ring theory)|nonunit]] element of <math display="inline">T_{A}</math> is a zero-divisor.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|52–53}}  Every overring of <math display="inline">R_{A}</math> contained in <math display="inline">T_{A}</math> is a ring <math display="inline">S_{A}</math>, and <math display="inline">S</math> is an overring of <math display="inline">R</math>.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|52–53}}  Ring <math display="inline">R_{A}</math> is [[Integral element|integrally closed]] in <math display="inline">T_{A}</math> if <math display="inline">R</math> is integrally closed in <math display="inline">T</math>.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|52–53}}

===Noetherian domain===
====Definitions====
{{see also|Regular element (disambiguation)}}
A <em>[[Noetherian ring]]</em> satisfies the 3 equivalent <em>[[Finite set|finitenss]] conditions</em> i) every [[Ascending chain condition|ascending chain]] of [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideals]] is finite, ii) every non-empty family of ideals has a [[Maximal and minimal elements|maximal element]] and iii) every ideal has a [[Hilbert's basis theorem|finite basis]].{{sfn|Zariski|Samuel|1965}}{{rp|199}}

An [[integral domain]] is a <em>[[Dedekind domain]]</em> if every ideal of the domain is a finite product of [[prime ideal]]s.{{sfn|Zariski|Samuel|1965}}{{rp|270}}

A ring's <em>restricted [[dimension]]</em> is the maximum [[Krull dimension|rank]] among the ranks of all prime ideals that contain a regular element.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|52}}

A ring <math display="inline">R</math> is <em>[[local ring|locally]] [[nilpotent]]free</em> if every ring <math display="inline">R_{M}</math> with [[maximal ideal]] <math display="inline">M</math> is free of nilpotent elements or a ring with every nonunit a [[zero divisor]].{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|52}}

An <em>[[affine ring]]</em> is the [[homomorphism|homomorphic]] [[Image (mathematics)|image]] of a [[polynomial ring]] (a [[finitely generated algebra]]) over a [[Field (mathematics)|field]].{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|58}}

====Properties====
Every overring of a Dedekind ring is a Dedekind ring.{{sfn|Cohen|1950}}{{sfn|Lane|Schilling|1939}}

Every overrring of a [[direct sum]] of rings whose non-unit elements are all zero-divisors is a Noetherian ring.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|53}}

Every overring of a [[Krull dimension|Krull]] 1-dimensional Noetherian domain is a Noetherian ring.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|53}}

These statements are equivalent for Noetherian ring <math display="inline">R</math> with integral closure <math display="inline">\bar{R}</math>.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|57}}
* Every overring of <math display="inline">R</math> is a Noetherian ring.
* For each maximal ideal <math display="inline">M</math> of <math display="inline">R</math>, every overring of <math display="inline">R_{M}</math> is a Noetherian ring.
* Ring <math display="inline">R</math> is locally nilpotentfree with restricted dimension 1 or less.
* Ring <math display="inline">\bar{R}</math> is Noetherian, and ring <math display="inline">R</math> has restricted dimension 1 or less.
* Every overring of <math display="inline">\bar{R}</math> is integrally closed.

These statements are equivalent for affine ring <math display="inline">R</math> with integral closure <math display="inline">\bar{R}</math>.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|58}}
* Ring <math display="inline">R</math> is locally nilpotentfree.
* Ring <math display="inline">\bar{R}</math> is a finite <math display="inline">R</math>-[[Module (mathematics)|module]].
* Ring <math display="inline">\bar{R}</math> is Noetherian.

An integrally closed local ring <math display="inline">R</math> is an integral domain or a ring whose non-unit elements are all zero-divisors.{{sfn|Davis|1962}}{{rp|58}}

A Noetherian integral domain is a Dedekind ring if every overring of the Noetherian ring is integrally closed.{{sfn|Davis|1964}}{{rp|198}}

Every overring of a Noetherian integral domain is a ring of fractions if the Noetherian integral domain is a Dedekind ring with a torsion class group.{{sfn|Davis|1964}}{{rp|200}}

===Coherent rings===
====Definitions====
A <em>[[coherent ring]]</em> is a commutative ring with each [[Glossary of ring theory|finitely generated]] ideal [[Glossary of ring theory|finitely presented]].{{sfn|Papick|1978}}{{rp|373}}  Noetherian domains and [[Prüfer domain]]s are coherent.{{sfn|Papick|1980}}{{rp|137}}

A <em>pair</em> <math display="inline">(R,T)</math> indicates an integral domain [[Glossary of ring theory|extension]] of <math display="inline">T</math> over <math display="inline">R</math>.{{sfn|Papick|1979}}{{rp|331}}

Ring <math display="inline">S</math> is an <em>intermediate</em> domain for pair <math display="inline">(R,T)</math> if <math display="inline">R</math> is a subdomain of <math display="inline">S</math> and <math display="inline">S</math> is a subdomain of <math display="inline">T</math>.{{sfn|Papick|1979}}{{rp|331}} 
====Properties====
A Noetherian ring's Krull dimension is 1 or less if every overring is coherent.{{sfn|Papick|1978}}{{rp|373}}

For integral domain pair <math display="inline">(R,T)</math>, <math display="inline">T</math> is an overring of <math display="inline">R</math> if each intermediate integral domain is integrally closed in <math display="inline">T</math>.{{sfn|Papick|1979}}{{rp|332}}{{sfn|Davis|1973}}{{rp|175}}

The integral closure of <math display="inline">R</math> is a Prüfer domain if each [[Subset|proper]] overring of <math display="inline">R</math> is coherent.{{sfn|Papick|1980}}{{rp|137}}

The overrings of Prüfer domains and Krull 1-dimensional Noetherian domains are coherent.{{sfn|Papick|1980}}{{rp|138}}

===Prüfer domains===
====Properties====
A ring has <em>QR property</em> if every overring is a localization with a multiplicative set.{{sfn|Fuchs|Heinzer|Olberding|2004}}{{rp|196}}  The QR domains are Prüfer domains.{{sfn|Fuchs|Heinzer|Olberding|2004}}{{rp|196}}  A Prüfer domain with a torsion [[Picard group]] is a QR domain.{{sfn|Fuchs|Heinzer|Olberding|2004}}{{rp|196}}  A Prüfer domain is a QR domain if the [[Radical of a ring|radical]] of every finitely generated ideal equals the radical generated by a [[principal ideal]].{{sfn|Pendleton|1966}}{{rp|500}}

The statement <math display="inline">R</math> is a [[Prüfer domain]] is equivalent to:{{sfn|Bazzoni|Glaz|2006}}{{rp|56}}
* Each overring of <math display="inline"> R</math>  is the [[Intersection (set theory)|intersection]] of localizations of <math display="inline"> R</math>,   and <math display="inline"> R</math> is integrally closed.
* Each overring of <math display="inline"> R</math>  is the intersection of rings of fractions of <math display="inline"> R</math>,   and <math display="inline"> R</math> is integrally closed.
* Each overring of <math display="inline"> R</math>  has prime ideals that are extensions of the prime ideals of <math display="inline"> R</math>, and <math display="inline"> R</math> is integrally closed.
* Each overring of <math display="inline"> R</math>  has at most 1 prime ideal lying over any prime ideal of <math display="inline"> R</math>,   and <math display="inline"> R</math> is integrally closed
* Each overring of <math display="inline"> R</math>  is integrally closed.
* Each overring of <math display="inline"> R</math>  is coherent.

The statement <math display="inline">R</math> is a [[Prüfer domain]] is equivalent to:{{sfn|Fontana|Papick|2002}}{{rp|167}}
* Each overring <math display>S</math> of <math display="inline">R</math> is [[Module (mathematics)|flat]] as a <math>S</math>-module.
* Each [[Valuation ring|valuation overring]] of <math display="inline">R</math> is a ring of fractions.

===Minimal overring===
====Definitions====
A <em>minimal ring homomorphism</em> <math display="inline">f</math> is an [[Injective function|injective]] non-[[Surjective function|surjective]] homomorophism, and if the homomorphism <math display="inline">f</math> is a composition of homomorphisms <math display="inline">g</math> and <math display="inline">h</math> then <math display="inline">g</math> or <math display="inline">h</math> is an isomorphism.{{sfn|Ferrand|Olivier|1970}}{{rp|461}}

A <em>proper minimal ring extension</em> <math display="inline">T</math> of subring <math display="inline">R</math> occurs if the ring [[Inclusion (set theory)|inclusion]] of <math display="inline">R</math> in to <math display="inline">T</math> is a minimal ring homomorphism.  This implies the ring pair <math display="inline">(R,T)</math> has no proper intermediate ring.{{sfn|Dobbs|Shapiro|2006}}{{rp|186}}

A <em>minimal overring</em> <math display="inline">T</math> of ring <math display="inline">R</math> occurs if <math display="inline">T</math> contains <math display="inline">R</math> as a subring, and the ring pair <math display="inline">(R,T)</math> has no proper intermediate ring.{{sfn|Dobbs|Shapiro|2007}}{{rp|60}}

The <em>Kaplansky ideal transform</em> (<em>Hayes transform</em>, <em>S-transform</em>) of ideal <math display="inline">I</math> with respect to integral domain <math display="inline">R</math> is a subset of the fraction field <math display="inline">Q(R)</math>.  This subset contains elements <math display="inline">x</math> such that for each element <math display="inline">y</math> of the ideal <math display="inline">I</math> there is a positive integer <math display="inline">n</math> with the product <math display="inline">x \cdot y^{n}</math> contained in integral domain <math display="inline">R</math>.{{sfn|Sato|Sugatani|Yoshida|1992}}{{sfn|Dobbs|Shapiro|2007}}{{rp|60}}

====Properties====
Any domain generated from a minimal ring extension of domain <math display="inline">R</math> is an overring of <math display="inline">R</math> if <math display="inline">R</math> is not a field.{{sfn|Sato|Sugatani|Yoshida|1992}}{{sfn|Dobbs|Shapiro|2006}}{{rp|186}}

The field of fractions of <math display="inline">R</math> contains minimal overring <math display="inline">T</math> of <math display="inline">R</math> when <math display="inline">R</math> is not a field.{{sfn|Dobbs|Shapiro|2007}}{{rp|60}}

Assume an integrally closed integral domain <math display="inline">R</math> is not a field,  If a minimal overring of integral domain <math display="inline">R</math> exists, this minimal overring occurs as the Kaplansky transform of a maximal ideal of <math display="inline">R</math>.{{sfn|Dobbs|Shapiro|2007}}{{rp|60}}

==Examples==
The [[Bézout domain|Bézout integral domain]] is a type of Prüfer domain; the Bézout domain's defining property is every finitely generated ideal is a principal ideal.  The Bézout domain will share all the overring properties of a Prüfer domain.{{sfn|Fontana|Papick|2002}}{{rp|168}}

The integer ring is a Prüfer ring, and all overrings are rings of quotients.{{sfn|Davis|1964}}{{rp|196}}  
The [[dyadic rational]] is a fraction with an integer numerator and power of 2 denominators.
The dyadic rational ring is the localization of the [[integer]]s by powers of two and an overring of the integer ring.
